newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-FELLOW PROS EYEING TIGER'S NEXT STEP AT U.S. OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-FELLOW PROS EYEING TIGER'S NEXT STEP AT U.S. OPEN.

text.p: All eyes will be trained on the Tiger at the U.S. Open championship starting on Thursday at Congressional Country Club -- and none more probing than the searching looks of Woods's fellow professionals.

The exploits of the amazing, 21-year-old Woods have certainly captivated golf fans and drawn newcomers to the sport, but his rivals are keenest to know how the Masters champion will fare on a rugged U.S. Open course.

"We're sort of anxious to see what's going to happen," said Briton Colin Montgomerie, the leading player on the European tour four years running. "Very anxious to see what's going to happen here compared to what transpired at Augusta."

What happened at Augusta National was that Woods overwhelmed the golf course and the field, setting records for lowest total and widest margin of victory with a 12-stroke triumph that made him the youngest Masters champion ever.
Augusta National is tailor-made for Woods, where length off the tee is rewarded and stray drives go generally unpunished on a layout bereft of rough.
Congressional offers up the longest ever Open course. The U.S. championship, however, always uses punishing rough to put a premium on accuracy and errant drives will cost strokes.
Montgomerie, one of golf's straightest drivers, has finished third and lost in a three-way playoff in past Opens.

"I think it was obvious to all that witnessed Augusta, that Tiger Woods was very comfortable playing that course," said Montgomerie, who Woods thumped by nine shots (65 to 74) in a third-round pairing at the Masters before the dispirited Briton limped home with a final-round 81 to finish tied for 30th.
"Here, it is different. It takes possibly his greatest asset, which is length, more out of the equation and gives us mere mortals more of an opportunity to compete.
"The playing field is more level here than it would be at an Augusta-type course set-up. So we're looking forward to how he's going to perform and how we're going to perform against him."
Woods knows Congressional poses an entirely different test.
"Driving is at a premium," acknowledged Woods, who said he plans on using his driver only three times from the tees to improve his likelihood of hitting fairways rather than rough.
"Whereas at Augusta, it was like a driving range -- bombs away on the driving."
His prodigious length, however, will still come in handy.

At the daunting, 475-yard par-4 sixth hole Woods needed only a 7-iron to reach the green in practice. Former British Open and PGA champion Nick Price, by contrast, hit driver and 1-iron, and twice British Open champion Greg Norman said he might lay up with his second shot to the converted par-5 hole.
Still, Woods differed with Montgomerie about the critical element in his game, which brought him three U.S. Junior and three U.S. Amateur titles before he turned pro.
"My mind is, I feel, the strongest part about me. The biggest asset I have is to be able to think myself around the golf course," he said.
"People don't see that. They look at the long drives. They look at the birdies, ball spinning back or making long putts. They look at that. But they don't look at the things that lead up to that.
"My dad has always preached to me: 'Play golf with your mind. Play golf intelligently. Don't beat yourself.'"

Woods, as always, said he expects to win this week, which would keep him on course for an assault on a Grand Slam sweep of golf's four major championships. He rattled off names of his leading rivals in the field of 156.

"As far as players that can win, I think you have to look at anyone who is playing hot right now," he said. "Justin Leonard is coming off a win last week and he's driving farther. He's a very straight hitter.
"Guys who hit the ball like that, like (Nick) Faldo. Greg (Norman) is playing very well right now. Tom Lehman, (Steve) Elkington. Colin Montgomerie is a great driver of the ball."
Win or lose, Woods will rate the year a success.

"I think '97 would be a great year, whether I win or lose. I have accomplished a lot of my goals already, and winning a major was something I've always wanted to do my entire life. Now I have three more chances, which is kind of nice. But just to win one, that's a dream come true."
Montgomerie is most interested in Woods's upcoming chance.
"We're all anxious to find out how he copes with this form of golf against the Augusta form of golf," the Briton said.
"I think if he copes with this and wins here, then we've all got to look somewhere else because if he's winning Augusta and here, then we're all in trouble."
